Indian philosophy makes valuable distinctions to this debate—knowledge and knower, mind and soul, intellect and consciousness, self-perception and other knowledge, doubt and lack. But no tradition should be made a mechanical answer-key to modern AI. The parallel method communicates, not imputation.

title: Evidence and Responsibility in the Age of AI
part: Science, Technology, the Digital World and AI
summary: Full chain of AI proof-responsibility Claim → Source → Origin-Chain → Version/Model → Process → Human Check → Decision → Impact → audit trail → Correction/Appeal → Liability Fluent Answer ≠ Proof ; automation ≠ responsibility-deletion ; “The model said” ≠ reasonable cause ; audit trail without decision = retest hard ; Admit error + correction + appeal = responsive system The basic assertion of this chapter is: in the AI ​​age, understand evidence as a “chain of origin”, not the “content of an answer”; And construct responsibility as “role-specific duties and ultimate accountability” rather than “blame on one person”. Verifiable sources, versioned processes, human authorization, audit trail, correction and appeal—they are elements of the same responsive knowledge system. First principle—AI output can be prima facie information, not self-evident evidence. In general brainstorming, verification can be light; high-stakes Have a mandatory level of independent scrutiny of original sources in medicine, law, finance, historical citations, academic references or public policy. Second principle—the burden of proof claim Change accordingly. “This book is famous” and “This sentence is on such and such a page” would not ask for the same verification. Numbers, dates, citations, legal provisions, pharmaceutical quantities, scientific results, attribution and archival claim demand high source-specificity.
source: Gajendra Thakur’s Parallel Philosophy, Volume II · supplied Maithili Chapter 89 · English translation
purvapaksha: First premise: “AI is more accurate on average than humans, so humans everywhere should be removed.” Average performance would not show context, subgroup, rare case and accountability cost. More accurate system can be useful, but failure mode, appeal, domain shift and harm severity checks are required for authority transfer. The second premise: “AI is only a tool; the responsibility belongs to the entire user.” Tool design, defaults, warnings, capability claims, deployment constraints and foreseeable misuse can generate developer/deployer duty. Hammer-simple tool analogies not always applicable to adaptive opaque systems. Third premise: “The model made the decision automatically, so no human is responsible.” The environment, objective, data access, threshold, deployment and authority of automatic decisions are determined by the human/organization. Autonomy can be an operational description, not an argument for an accountability vacuum. Fourth premise: “The source is given, so the answer is authentic.” source existence Only the first stage. relevant passage, exact quotation, source authority, date, context, conflicting sources and inference validity to be checked. Fifth premise: “explainable AI solves all problems.” explanation fidelity, comprehensibility, audience, manipulability and causal relevance questioned. Beautiful explanation would not legitimize unjust policy.
uttarapaksha: First rule of the answer—classify the claim. General interpretation, exact fact, number, quotation, diagnosis, legal interpretation, prediction, recommendation, ranking, eligibility decision—all have different evidence thresholds. the system interface should show the user this distinction. Second rule—create source ladder. primary document/original data high priority; reputable secondary analysis Next; tertiary summary auxiliary; uncited AI prose only navigation/brainstorming. The more important the claim, the higher the source in the ladder. Third rule—citation verification Both automatic + human. Can check URL/DOI existence check, quoted string match, publication metadata, date freshness machine; Check semantic relevance, context and controversial interpretation human/expert. Fourth rule—keep provenance log minimum dataset: timestamp, model/version, system configuration, user prompt or case identifier, retrieved source IDs, tool actions, decision rule, human reviewer, final action. privacy-sensitive field remain access-controlled. Fifth Rule—high-stakes decisions should have a “reason for action” structured. Who evidence considered, who excluded, key rule/threshold, uncertainty, human reviewer, available appeal. generic “system determined” not because.
synthesis: In the AI ​​age, proof only means “Where is the link?”. No; How the claims originated, what sources/models/versions were used, what human judgments were involved, what uncertainties remained, and how revisions were possible—this entire series forms the modern form of proof. Responsibility is also not just blame. Without role-specific duty, competent oversight, traceability, monitoring, incident response, correction and appeal, the words “human in the loop” or “ethical AI” can remain empty. The most dangerous sentence can be—“the system said so.” This sentence takes the place of the cause, but not the cause; takes the form of authority, but not legitimacy. The proper questions are: why is the system configured like this, what is the evidence, who is the reviewer, who is the decision authority, who will correct if there is harm? The Indian Pramanamimansa and the Nyaya-Navyanyaya tradition of Mithila teach modern AI governance an important lesson: go through the scrutiny of knowledge claims for means, faults, doubts, scope, titles, counterparts and rebuttals. Modern audit is not a mechanical copy of this ancient discipline, but a parallel reworking.

title: A Second Form of Multi-Source Rationalism
part: Parallel Philosophy in the Twenty-First Century
summary: Multievidence Discretionism 2.0 — Cycle of Evidence-Balancing Assertion → Question-Split → Source-Diversity → Source-Independence → Quality/Relevance → Conflicting Evidence → Weighting → Tentative Conclusion → Retest Multiple Sources ≠ Equal Weight; multiple citations ≠ independent confirmation ; Experience ≠ self-determining; number ≠ value-free ; AI output ≠ proof ; Revision ≠ Defeat is the basic assertion of this chapter: Open many possible sources of evidence on truth claims, but treat them all as equal opinions; Give claim-specific weight by examining evidence of each source’s capabilities, limitations, independence, relevance, and constraints; Write the conclusion with tentative clarity and accept revisions on new evidence. First principle—abundance of evidence is not merely abundance of sources. The number of proofs did not increase if the same basic material was repeated in ten forms. independent pathways, different measurement methods, different institutional sources or different types of evidence can increase the value of real confirmation. Second principle—Split the claim. Outcome, cause, fairness, cost, public meaning and historical comparison can be separate claims within a sentence like “this policy is a failure”. each A sub-claim requires separate proof. Without claim division, the correct weight of evidence is not possible.
source: Gajendra Thakur’s Parallel Philosophy, Volume II · supplied Maithili Chapter 90 · English translation
purvapaksha: The first premise: “Assuming multiple proofs will make all views equally true.” No. Multiple validity accepts source plurality, not equal validity. forgery, contradiction, poor method, dependency, irrelevance and defeated inference reduce the burden of proof. Second premise: “One gold standard is sufficient; all others are weak.” In some domains, high-quality methods might be superior, but complex claims would have multiple levels. not eliminating all questions of trial patient experience of treatment efficacy, implementation context, rare harm and cost ethics. Third antecedent: “Direct experience best; the rest mediated.” Direct also selected, approach-relative and limited. not in direct view of distant events, microorganisms, past or population patterns; instrument, testimony, inference necessary. Fourth premise: “Personal experience is subjective, so not knowledge.” subjective aspect could be part of the fact itself. The phenomenology of pain or humiliation is not completely replaced by observer-independent measurement. Question experience not reject, claim scope to clarify. Fifth premise: “Big data eliminates bias.” large N would not correct systematic measurement error, nonrepresentative coverage, historical exclusion or bad labels. Increasing the biased process scale could reinforce the bias.
uttarapaksha: First rule of the answer—create a claim sheet: exact claim, scope, time, population, key terms, stakes, required precision. Evidence search directionless without vague claims being clear. Second rule—create a source-map. primary, secondary, testimony, quantitative, qualitative, archival, experimental, digital, AI-assisted—write separately which sources would support which sub-claims. Third rule—put independence tag: original, derivative, common-source, correlated method. Don't count five common-source reports as five independent confirmations. Fourth rule—quality checklist: authenticity, competence, method, sampling, measurement, date, completeness, conflict, reproducibility, correction record. quality score not a mechanical final truth, but a means of structured attention. Fifth rule—relevance test: Exactly how much of the claim does the evidence speak to? not the person-situation of the national average local village; one anecdote not national prevalence. scope mismatch Write clearly.
synthesis: The second form of multiproof rationality is an attempt to combine both democratization and rigor of knowledge. Multiple sources have the right to speak, but not each claim has the same weight. The burden should be determined by claims, quality, independence, relevance, evidence of obstacles and risk. The most important prohibitions of this method are three: numbers are not synonymous with truth; Experience is not synonymous with universal reason; Institutional authority is not synonymous with infallibility. While rejecting these three, numbers, experience and expertise can all be given due place. Not the 2.0 determinism of rationalism. He registers uncertainty, has the courage to say “unknown”, and accepts the revision trigger earlier. Strong ideas are not those that never change; Strong ideas are those that keep the rules of change clear. Indian authentic mysticism, the jurisprudence-neojudicial question-discipline of Mithila, modern science, history, social research and digital verification are not the same tradition; But in parallel dialogue, they all teach one lesson—claims must pass the scrutiny of means, faults, counter-arguments, limitations, and reexamination.

title: Coexistential Realism after the Linguistic Turn
part: Parallel Philosophy in the Twenty-First Century
summary: Coexistential realism — relation-map of reality, language and practice Reality → experience/resistance → concept → naming → statement → social practice/institution → action → re-encountering reality Language is not the sole creator of reality; Language is not passive nameplate either ; The description may be many ; Not all descriptions are equally adequate ; Social reality may depend on linguistic behavior; Natural resistance does not end with linguistic agreement. The first formula of coexistent realism is: reality is multilayered, not uniform. The physical, biological, perceptual, interpersonal, institutional, historical, symbolic and digital levels would be interconnected but not have the same type of dependency. The word “existence” is not the name of the same causal formula at all levels. Second formula: there is a field of resistance independent of language. Not entirely determined by my naming of stones, rain, bodies, pathogens, geography, physical boundaries or biological processes. We can give the wrong name, but objective resistance can eventually get the wrong name into trouble. Third thread: linguistic mediation is real. The outside world Though free, human beings understand them through concepts, comparisons, measurements, memories, stories, calculations and communication. Therefore, “completely unbiased description” would not automatically follow from “independent reality”.
source: Gajendra Thakur’s Parallel Philosophy, Volume II · supplied Maithili Chapter 91 · English translation
purvapaksha: First premise: If access to the world is always through language/concept, then talk of language-independent reality is meaningless. Claiming the existence of something that can never be seen without mediation is unnecessary metaphysics. The second premise: “resistance” is also a linguistic interpretation. Calling the experiment a failure, calling the data an anomaly, or calling the object “the same”—all conceptual judgments. So the appeal of resistance could not save realism. Third premise: social categories are clearly power-laden; Therefore, the language of truth can become a way to legitimize power structures. Saying “real” risks provisional social order being declared natural. Fourth premise: Neutral comparison between different conceptual schemes is not possible. Each scheme creates its own criteria, proofs and ontology; So where does the “external” criterion come from to say one is more adequate than the other? Fifth premise: Full respect for linguistic plurality is possible only if truth is considered community-specific. Universal realism often imposes the category of the dominant language on the weaker language.
uttarapaksha: First answer: mediation would not prohibit existence. We reach by telescope, microscope, statistics, memory, language and equipment; mediated access does not mean invented object. The question is not “whether there is mediation”, but “how does mediation work and what error does it bring”. Second answer: there are interpretations of resistance, but not all interpretations would yield the same results. A model that fails repeated intervention, a prediction that breaks down repeatedly, a pattern that does not match the archival claim provenance—that pattern of failure puts additional pressure on interpretation. Third answer: realism is not equivalent to naturalization. Social categories can indeed be historical/political, and realism can check their causal effect for precisely this reason. Saying “this category exists” is not saying “it is eternal/just”. ontology and normativity are separate questions. Fourth answer: conceptual schemes are not completely closed islands. shared body, environment, causal interaction, translation practice, successful coordination, prediction, pain, resource constraints and material traces provide a partial basis for cross-scheme comparison. neutrality not complete, equivalence nevertheless possible. Fifth answer: Linguistic justice does not mean communalization of truth. Respect for minority language/local knowledge requires listening to its concepts, sources, experiences and categories; But not every empirical claim is exempt from countertesting. Respect and criticism can coexist.
synthesis: The lasting achievement of the linguistic turn is that the naïve belief in language as an impartial window was broken. They choose words, form classes, expose/conceal relationships, perform social actions and carry power. Omitting this achievement would re-simplify realism. But when extremist forms of linguistic turn merge reality into language, it is difficult to understand the possibility of resistance, body, nature, causal structure, non-linguistic experience and misrepresentation of the world. Coexistential realism re-establishes the pressure of the “outside” on this boundary. The central thread of this chapter is: reality is multilayered; Language is a powerful level and medium of it, not the entire source. Social facts are real even though they are constructed, natural facts are not language-constructed even though they are described, and individuals/communities are more than categories even though they fall into categories. Realism not monochromaticism here. Many visions, languages ​​and models can capture different relations of the same world. Plurality is not mere relativism, as the criteria of evidence, resistance, consequence, coherence, translation, intervention and revision check the description remains.

title: Dignity-Based Ethics and New Identities
part: Parallel Philosophy in the Twenty-First Century
summary: Dignity-Based Ethics — Relationship-Map of Person, Identity and Institutional Behavior Person → Body/Experience → Self-Description → Relationship → Social Identity → Institutional Classification → Rights/Opportunities → Recognition/Dishonor → Resistance/Modification → Re-Self-Construction Dignity Inseparable moral boundary; Identity is multi-layered and variable ; Self-identification is important but not all-evidence-contradictory; Social categories have real impact but not the entirety of the individual; Respect does not mean prohibition of criticism; The institution should bear the responsibility for the reasons for classification, loss, appeal and correction. Formula One: Dignity is the minimum moral value of a person, not a reward. Dignity would not be earned by talent, success, position, wealth, popularity, moral excellence or social usefulness; For this reason, even failed, dependent, unpopular or crime-accused individuals are entitled to protection from humiliation, torture, dehumanization and arbitrary treatment. Second formula: dignity and innocence are not the same. A person can do wrong and be held liable; Still, there will be limits to punishment, criticism or ban. Responsibility would not eliminate dignity. third Formula: Dignity and reputation are different. Reputation can be increased or decreased by social evaluation; Dignity is the moral baseline. Without this distinction, popular individuals may be perceived as more morally valuable and stigmatized individuals as less valuable.
source: Gajendra Thakur’s Parallel Philosophy, Volume II · supplied Maithili Chapter 92 · English translation
purvapaksha: Premise 1: “Dignity” is an extremely vague term; Different people take different meanings, so making it a moral basis is pointless. Premise 2: If all persons have equal dignity, how to make moral distinctions? If criminals, doctors, children, judges and con men are all equally valuable, wouldn't responsibility be blurred? Premise 3: Identity is self-declaration. Seeking external proof or institutional categories is an attack on the autonomy of the individual. Premise 4: Conversely, identity is only an objective fact. Things like self-descriptions, experiences or beliefs are feelings only; Policy should rest on measurable categories only. Premise 5: Group-based justice clashes with person-dignity. If the individual is central, then questions of historical group-injustice or representation will be morally secondary.
uttarapaksha: Answer 1: The concept should not be omitted because it is unclear; operational criteria should be created. In this chapter, dignity gives at least five prohibitions/obligations: no dehumanization, no arbitrary domination, no total neglect of basic interests, no unnecessary prohibition of voices/reasons, and no reduction of persons to mere scores/categories. This criterion does not end the controversy, but it provides a common basis for reasoning. Answer 2: Equal dignity not equal outcomes or roles. Punishment on evidence of guilt, rights based on expertise, custodial decisions for children—all are possible. Equal dignity only limits the distinction to relevant reason, proportionate process and respect for human-values. Answer 3: Priority of self-description and verification of public facts can coexist. There may be more first-party authority in name/experience/personal sense; External evidence plays an increasing role in legal entitlement, historical claim, biological/medical questions or binding influence on others. domain distinction reduces contention. Answer 4: The measurable category also consists of conceptual judgments. What variable to measure, where to put threshold, How to fill in missing data, which proxy to use—these can be social/ethical choices. objectivity does not mean “zero human judgment”, but a transparent examination of judgment. Answer 5: Individuals and groups are not mutually exclusive levels. Group-based injustice produces patterned effects on individuals; Therefore, reform policy can use group evidence. But the design of the remedy should not imprison the person in a stereotype, it is the limit of dignity.
synthesis: Dignity-based ethics regards the individual as neither a self-contained atom separate from society, nor a component of the community/database. Individuals are embodied, related, historicized, dependent, changeable and participatory entities of reason/experience. Reducing this complexity to a score or an innate label can create moral disadvantage. The first achievement of the new identity is multi-layeredness. Self-awareness, social recognition, legal status, pedigree, somatic facts and digital model are not the same thing. Identifying the first level in the dispute removes many confusions. The second achievement is modifiability. Individuals change, institutions make mistakes, categories become outdated, new evidence of history is found. Without correction/appeal, identity rule can become a harsh fate. The third achievement is the coexistence of truth and respect. The dignity of a person would not make all his assertions automatically true; And a person would not be dishonored if a claim is proven wrong. It is this distinction that makes both rigorous evidence-testing and decent public life possible.

title: Polycentric Democracy and Network Power
part: Parallel Philosophy in the Twenty-First Century
summary: Polycentric Democracy — Relationship-Map of Power, Networks, Institutions and Citizen Responsibility Citizens → Local Bodies → State → Courts → Markets → Forums/Networks → Expert Institutions → Community → Media → Data-Systems → Mutual Control → Appeal/Reform → Shared Responsibility Central power not enough; Fragmented power is not automatically democratic ; Network not fair ; locality be valuable but exclusion-free ; The private forum may have public influence ; Authority requires reasons, limitations, appeals and audits ; Polycentrism is both cooperation and control First formula: polycentric democracy means not only many centres; Legitimate centers have mutual boundaries, cooperation, monitoring and appeal-relationships. If multiple power centers collide without rules, it is not a polycentric democracy, but a fragmented domination. Second thread: Power is not just the ability to give orders; There is also power to set agendas, open/close access, increase/decrease visibility, create standards, control data, classify, determine protocols and change the cost of options. Third formula: For each powerhouse jurisdiction be clear. what decisions are in his power, and what are not; what rights are minimally inviolable; and who will conduct the final/interim review in the dispute—it should be public.
source: Gajendra Thakur’s Parallel Philosophy, Volume II · supplied Maithili Chapter 93 · English translation
purvapaksha: Premise 1: Polycentricity slows down decisions. In a crisis action may be impossible due to multiple veto points, consultations and appeals. Premise 2: Citizens want clear responsible government. Too much center will increase blame shifting and weaken electoral accountability. Premise 3: Local self-government increases inequality. Wealthy towns will provide excellent service, poor areas will lag behind; National equality will be broken. Premise 4: Expert bodies are anti-democratic because officials are not elected. Premise 5: Imposing public obligations on private platforms will undermine innovation and freedom of expression.
uttarapaksha: Answer 1: Temporary command may be necessary in a crisis, but speed and accountability can be added by having pre-defined emergency competence, time limits, reporting and ex post review. Polycentrism would not demand infinite consultation on every decision. Answer 2: Blame shifting can be reduced by responsibility mapping. Each chain should state decision owner, data provider, technical vendor, approving authority, appeal body and oversight body. A decision can have multiple responsible parties, yet “none” is not acceptable. Answer 3: Fiscal equalization with decentralization, national minimum standards, targeted grants and capacity support necessary. Local discretion does not mean complete dependence on local resource-luck. Answer 4: The legitimacy of expert bodies consists of delegated law, competence, conflict rules, transparent method, legislative/judicial review and public reason. Not being elected, such a body is not void legitimate; But unchecked expert rule is also not appropriate. Answer 5: obligation be proportional. Small private forum and not the same burden on the dominant infrastructure platform. Liability should increase on the basis of public impact, market power, dependency, risk and substitutability.
synthesis: The main achievement of polycentric democracy is the understanding that democracy would not be defended simply by finding the “right centre”. Modern power is distributed in many places; Therefore, a network of accountability should also be established in many places. Polycentrism is not a simple synonym for decentralization. Local institutions, states, courts, regulators, markets, platforms, communities and expert bodies may each have legitimate territories; But each needs limits, reasons, transparency, appeal and higher/lateral review. Network-entities reside in physical/technological structures—protocol, ranking, identity, payment, cloud, contract, data, reputation. Such a power could not go beyond the democratic question by saying “private,” especially when the basic opportunities of the citizen depend on it. Also, it is not appropriate to turn all private influence into state bureaucratic control. Many tools available like proportional obligation, interoperability, independent oversight, competition, collective voice, judicial remedy and open standards.

title: Rational Religious Pluralism in a Post-Secular Society
part: Parallel Philosophy in the Twenty-First Century
summary: Relationship-Map of Religion, Irreligion, Public Conscience, Equal Citizenship and Coexistence Conscience → Faith/Non-Faith → Tradition → Community → Public Reason → Equal Citizenship → Constitutional Rights → Non-Dominant State → Dialogue/Translation → Dissent → Appeal → Peaceful Coexistence Religion is not automatically private; The state is not automatically impartial ; Plurality is not mere toleration ; Similarity not uniformity ; Public reason not anti-religious language ; Faith is not beyond criticism ; Disbelief is not an inferior choice ; Post-secularism would not have eliminated the secular constitutional floor ; The final criterion—dignity, free conscience, non-discrimination, non-violence, causal responsibility, appeal and common citizenship. Formula One: Freedom of conscience is a fundamental right. A person can believe in religion, change, learn from many traditions, be skeptical, or believe in no religion. The state or community is not the essential master of his conscience. Second Sutra: Freedom of religion is not just entering places of worship; It is associated with questions of faith, practice, organization, teaching, symbols, celebration, food, clothing, silence, conversion and apostasy. But this The limits of liberty are equal rights with other persons, bodily integrity, public safety and non-discrimination. Formula 3: Freedom from religion is also part of freedom of religion. Citizens should not be forced into religious ceremonies, proclamations, fees, education or identification. The “majority tradition” does not make coercion voluntary.
source: Gajendra Thakur’s Parallel Philosophy, Volume II · supplied Maithili Chapter 94 · English translation
purvapaksha: Premise 1: Religion is essentially irrational belief; It has no place in the public sphere. Post-secularism will turn the scientific society backwards. Premise 2: If religion is true, then the state has a moral obligation to support true religion. Giving equal status to false beliefs is an artificial equalization of truth and falsehood. Premise 3: secular neutrality impossible; Each state is based on some comprehensive worldview. So it is more honest to openly accept the majority religion. Premise 4: The “translation” of public reason is the colonial pressure of secular language on religious citizens. Turning the reason for faith into irreligious words destroys his soul. Premise 5: Community rights are above individualism; Tradition creates individuals. Too much emphasis on individual exit or dissent will disintegrate the community.
uttarapaksha: Answer 1: The word “religious” itself is not synonymous with irrationality. Religious claims consist of metaphysical beliefs, historical facts, moral arguments, experiences, symbols and community practices at different levels. public policy can check the empirical claim; can avoid state coercion on metaphysical conviction; It is possible to debate the public consequences of moral reasons. Answer 2: Conviction on the truth is a right of the individual; State coercion not proof of truth. Different citizens believe opposites ultimate truth, and the institution of democracy is to create a peaceful equal citizenship amidst such disputes. Let the search for truth be open; coercive monopoly should be stopped. Answer 3: Neutrality is not a complete value-absence, it is a constitutional partiality—the advocacy of dignity, equality, freedom, due process, non-violence and civil reciprocity. This is not comprehensive theology; There is a political floor that can coexist with different life-views. Answer 4: Translation does not mean abandoning the original religious language. The citizen may say that his moral inspiration came from religion; When making policy, he should also state that the proposal is a civil rights, What common cause of health, environment, justice or public interest is fulfilled? Answer 5: The community is a source of development for the individual, but the individual is not the property of the community alone. voluntary belonging, internal voice, fair exit and external rights review not destroy the community; can strengthen legitimacy.
synthesis: The sane plurality of religions is not a metaphysical declaration of “all religions equally true”. It is a politico-moral system in which citizens may have different ultimate beliefs, yet share the same dignity, conscience, law, causal responsibility and non-violent dissent. A post-secular society is not an abandonment of secular constitutional achievement. On the contrary, he acknowledges that both religious and non-religious citizens are permanent in the modern public sphere; Therefore, secularism has to become a fair constitutional framework, not an exclusionary ideology. The task of the state is not to decide metaphysical truth; There is securing civil rights, limiting coercion, providing equal services, preventing violence, making fair accommodations, providing remedies for discrimination and providing reasons for public decisions. The legitimacy of religious communities comes not only from antiquity, numbers or sacred claims; The dignity of its members, dissent, rights of women/children, financial accountability, non-violence and reciprocity of other citizens should also be checked with respect.

title: The Parallel View of History: Genealogy, Archive and Evidence
part: Parallel Philosophy in the Twenty-First Century
summary: Relationship-map of events, relics, records, silences, classifications, source-review and modifiable history Event/Process → Remains → Selection → Recording → Preservation/Destruction → Classification → Archives → Search → Source-review → Mutual-confirmation → Counterparts → Interpretation → Public claims → Revision History Only winners' stories Not ; Archives are not merely impartial warehouses ; Silence itself is not absolute proof ; Genealogy is not about finding origin-purity, but about seeing accidental creations, entities, classifications and breakdowns; However, the entity would not make the evidence arbitrary ; Historical claims will be tied to source sources, dates, authorial status, context, textual tradition, independent corroboration, adverse evidence, material remains and revisable public reasoning; Parallel historiographies add marginalized voices, but do not remove the criterion of proof. First formula: past irrevocable, historiography modifiable. Events cannot change, but available evidence, questions, methods and interpretations can. Saying “history changed” should often be understood as knowledge structures being modified, not as the past being changed. Second formula: not the source event. Order, letter, inscription, report or autobiography one on event There is vision. The historian should distinguish between source claim, source production and underlying event. Third clue: Archives are selection machine. record creation, retention, cataloguing, declassification, destruction, digitization and search interfaces all form historical visibility.
source: Gajendra Thakur’s Parallel Philosophy, Volume II · supplied Maithili Chapter 95 · English translation
purvapaksha: Premise 1: archive creates entity; Therefore, archive-based history is merely a reproduction of power, objective truth impossible. Premise 2: genealogy proving every “truth” power-effect; Therefore, an independent criterion of proof does not survive. Premise 3: Marginal voices survived only in oral memory centuries later; Asking for documentary corroboration is elite bias. Premise 4: It would be a fair correction to assume the opposite of the history that the winner would have written. Premise 5: Multiple sources always contradictory; Ultimately, the historian's ideology decides what kind of story to choose.
uttarapaksha: Answer 1: archive could be power-constructed, but not completely arbitrary. Different power-center records, physical traces, foreign/neighbor archives, private papers, dates, material constraints challenging each other. archive critique is an expansion of truth-seeking, not an abandonment. Answer 2: genealogy showing historical conditions of truth-claims; This would not logically prove “all claims are false”. The claim of genealogy itself also relies on evidence, chronology, textual reading and counter-evidence—so the criterion of proof must be accepted to avoid self-contradiction. Answer 3: corroboration does not mean oral source taking permission from elite text. independent oral accounts, material landscape, family objects, demographic patterns, local vocabulary, later institutional effects also corroboration. Could change criteria according to source-type, not truthfulness. Answer 4: “The opposite of the winner = truth” mirror dogmatism. oppressed actor could also create memory error, factional interest, later myth. Applying the just history evidence standard to all actors, on unequal archival keeping survival in mind. Answer 5: ideology choosing questions, affecting language, but not eliminating evidence constraint. Historian's interpretation may be different, but impossible chronology, forged document, mistranslation, contradicted data may be caught. disagreement is degrees of freedom, not total freedom.
synthesis: The parallel history-view changes the focus of history, without removing the criterion of truth. Adding registers, letters, oral memory, material trace, language, ecology, women/disadvantaged experiences, digital records to the state archive—but checking the error mode of each source. Genealogical methods are not about finding “true origins”; Current categories are created, dismantled, institutionalized, forgotten alternatives and opening up feedback. The meaning of constructed history is not fictional; contingent reality. The archives would start before the archive room: what records were created, what survived, what was cataloged, what was digitized. silence This could be the result of the whole process. Silence is important, but not allowed to fill in the blanks with the desired story. disciplined inference resting on expected-record pattern, parallel source, material trace, oral convergence and explicit uncertainty.

title: Self-Critique: How Can Parallel Philosophy Accept Its Own Deconstruction?
part: Parallel Philosophy in the Twenty-First Century
summary: Seven Mirrors of Self-Criticism: Evidence, Reality, Dignity, Power, Religion, History and Self-Criticism Claims → Opponents → Weak Points → Alternative Explanations → Evidence of Obstacles → Experience of Affected Person → Revision → Reexamination The self-review of parallel philosophy is not decorative modesty; This is the seventh foundation of his method. If the evidence changes, the conclusion will change; If the language hides unseen hierarchies, the language will improve; If victim experience shows unexplored aspects of the theory, the theory will be rewritten; If the opposing argument is strong, it will not be won by presenting it as weak. The self-review of parallel philosophy is not self-destructive; is self-modification. Fragmentation does not mean nullifying each theory, but seeing the dualities, hierarchies, silences, exceptions, power relations and linguistic presuppositions hidden within them; followed by evidence-based reconstruction. The basic formula for self-review: “Hold your theories to the same criterion as you hold opposing theories.” If opposing sources Ask for the origin-chain, ask also for your source; If we check the limits of the opposition (generalisation), also of our own (generalisation); If you see the conflict of interest of the opposition, also look at your own institutional incentives. The order of fragmentation and reconstruction is not different: read → identify claims → define terms → find absent parties → build strongest counter-example → check independence of evidence → listen to experiences of affected parties → build alternative models → write (provisional) conclusions → declare revision-signal.
source: Gajendra Thakur’s Parallel Philosophy, Volume II · supplied Maithili Chapter 96 · English translation
purvapaksha: Premise 1: If philosophy doubts itself all the time, judgment will be impossible. Premise 2: Strong theories require stable roots; Revision openness will dissolve its identity. Premise 3: External criticism over lived experience is a repetition of domination. Premise 4: Multiple authenticity would eventually favor the experts, since ordinary citizens would not be able to check all sources. Antecedents 5: The task of the genealogical method is not to find truth, but to expose power; Adding realism would reduce its radical power.
uttarapaksha: Answer 1: Doubt and not anti-decision. Closing-rules, evidence limit-points and (reversible/irreversible) decision distinctions would make decisions possible. Accepting uncertainty and making decisions is common in science, justice and policy. Answer 2: Identity would be formed by (problem-solving) (commitments), not by the number of static formulas. If the original—evidence, dignity, public reason, modification—had survived, changing the (specific) (formulation) would have kept the tradition alive. Answer 3: The distinctive rights of lived experience should be acknowledged; The external check is not to deny its existence, but to check the limits of the causal/(general) claim. Apart from the insults of experience and the critical interpretation of experience. Answer 4: Expertise required, but (layered) transparency could be created—brief public reasons + technical (appendix) + original-source access + independent testing. Citizens need a way to (contest) not all the calculations. Answer 5: It is possible to uncover power and seek truth simultaneously. If entity-theories themselves made factual claims—who classified them, when, what effects—then they would need proof. The power of (radical) criticism increases, not decreases from the factual (discipline).
synthesis: Self-criticism, the seventh foundation of parallel philosophy, is not the safety shield of its entire system, but the open door. Saying protection-shield will again indicate (immunity); The door says—new evidence, opposing arguments, unheard of experiences, linguistic corrections, historical documents and technological changes may come inside. Self-fragmentation does not mean destroying one's principles. fragmentation showing hidden structure; changing self-review evidence (weight); Reconstruction forming revised doctrine. The three stages together would form philosophy (neither) (dogma) (nor) nihilism. Multiproof rationalism will itself check proof (dependence); coexistent realism level (confusion) checks; Checking vague dignity-based moralism; Polycentric democracy will check accountability gaps; religious majority coercion/(minority-within-minority) checking; The parallel history-view will check the redundancy of the archival (suspicion); Self-review will check your performativity. The joint thread of this chapter: “The power of parallel philosophy lies not in the fact that it will always be right; Write, revise, and be open to re-examination.”

title: Structure Exists, but Structure Is Not Destiny
summary: Structure–Action Cycle: Boundary → Opportunity → Practice → Resistance → Collective Action → Institutional Change → New Boundary Structure → Situation/Resources → Possible Alternatives → Actor → Feedback → Reward → Change in Rules/Institutions/Habits → Modified Structure Humans do not make decisions in a vacuum. Language, family, race, class, gender, schools, laws, markets, technology, geography, memories, institutions and historical heritage make up his sphere of choice. But this would not exhaust the options. The formula of parallel philosophy is: structure is real, but structure is not destiny; The doer is real, but the doer is not baseless omnipotence. The parallel philosophy of structure considers not “invisible forces yielding fixed fruits”, but relational configurations of repeated rules, resource-distribution, roles, expectations, networks, technological (affordance), punishment-rewards and institutional memory. This configuration changes the probability distribution; not determining the outcome of each individual. Agency is not pure will outside the structure. Doership means deciding between available/conceivable options, new interpretations of rules, cooperation, Disagreement, resistance, innovation, migration, (bargaining), institution-building and creating new habits. Agents would be born into structures, use the language of structures, yet be able to change structures. The parallel view uses the language of “structured probability” instead of determinism. For example, poverty makes higher education difficult—this could be a causal claim; “Poor students will not be able to get higher education” is the fatalistic claim. finding first claim interference; closing another future.
source: Gajendra Thakur’s Parallel Philosophy, Volume II · supplied Maithili Chapter 97 · English translation
purvapaksha: Premise 1: If structure is not destiny, then the term “structural injustice” will be weakened. Premise 2: Could become victim-blaming. Antecedent 3: Structural Explanation The person will (excuse) the culprit. Premise 4: Saying everything is multilevel would make the policy unclear. Premise 5: (merit) After all, there is the ability of the person.
uttarapaksha: Answer: No. Structural injustice does not claim to decide every outcome of the individual; Systematically, there are claims that opportunities, risks, respect or resources are unequally distributed. (probabilistic) effects also morally serious. Answer: Not victim-blaming, if the bondage, force and (resource) gaps are kept clear. It would also diminish dignity to regard victims as merely passive objects. Answer: Explanation and (justification) different. Social (pressure) could explain the cause of violence, not correct violence. The (degree) of (culpability) could vary according to the context. Answer: Multileveling does not prevent interference (priority). Leverage (point) could be chosen according to impact (size), (feasibility), authority, cost, (reversibility) and (distribution). Answer: Ability real, but creating opportunities, training, language, (nutrition), time, testing (design) and (inherited) (advantage) (performance). It is an illusion to regard (merit) as context-(free) (substance).
synthesis: “Structure is there, but structure is not destiny” is not just the optimistic slogan of parallel philosophy; It is the discipline of causation. It states that social patterns are real, measurable, and morally significant; But that would not make the person a completely predictable object. Respect for authority does not mean denying structural (injustice). On the contrary, recognizing injustice aims to increase the actual range of agency—more information, resources, safety, voice, (exit), reconsideration rights, (association) and the ability to change institutions. The criterion for structural reform is not just average outcomes: whose options increased? Whose (risk) decreased? Whose (voice) did you hear? Whose dignity is protected? On whom did the new (burden) fall? Is the correction (reversible/contestable)? Chapter 96 Self-Criticism teaches that philosophy itself is not beyond criticism. Chapter 97 is the social extension of that: no institution, tradition, class, technology or historical (arrangement) can be declared destined by saying that it “has been going on this way”.

title: Language Is a Limit, but Not a Prison
summary: Language–Reality Dialogue Cycle: Experience → Naming → Classification → Statement → Counterargument → Translation → Redescription → Modified Experience Language is a basic medium of the human world. We see things, make distinctions, form memories, ask for reasons, name justice and injustice, write history and plan for the future—language is active in all of this. But saying that language is active is not the same as saying that language is the ultimate creator of everything. Parallel philosophy emphasizes this distinction. The word “boundary” is used in this chapter to mean a shaping horizon, not just a restriction. Language clarifies some distinctions, blurs others; making some experiences worth sharing, others reducing the subtlety of the experience. But borders are mobile—new words, translations, science, poetry, law, vernacular, multilingual dialogue, pictures, signs, numbers and counterarguments change their lines. The parallel philosophy views language as a means of “mediated reality”. Reality might have dimensions independent of language, but human shared knowledge would often be organized by concepts, signs, measurements, names, documents and stories. For this reason, language is also a condition of knowledge and of criticism The subject, too. Language is the limit because each word makes some distinctions and cuts some continuity. When I say “forest,” I would identify an area, but within a forest, the complexities of water, soil, microbes, animals, human use, legal boundaries and seasonal changes would be summed up in one word. Categories are useful summaries, not the entire reality. Language is not a prison because humans could critique their vocabulary, create new words, change old meanings, grasp from other languages, explain unknown things by metaphors, and resort to pictures/numbers/examples/corporeal demonstrations when words fail.
source: Gajendra Thakur’s Parallel Philosophy, Volume II · supplied Maithili Chapter 98 · English translation
synthesis: “Language is a frontier, but not a prison” is the linguistic politeness formula of parallel philosophy. Difficult to share philosophy without language; Reality does not end with language alone. Words would give me paths to objects, experiences and society, but each path with choices, deductions and perspectives. For this reason, the philosophical task is not to police words, but to clarify the boundaries of meaning, to recognize historical change, to explain the harms/benefits of translation, to see the silences and powers, and to check claims with extralinguistic/independent evidence. Language-independent full vision could be out of human reach; However, by multiple languages, multiple methodologies, measurements, experiences, counterarguments and redescriptions, we can avoid becoming prisoners of a single terminology. Chapter 96 opening self-criticism, Chapter 97 saying structure is not destiny, and Chapter 98 applying this idea to language: linguistic structure is real, but man could change its limits through translation, new words, education, art, science, criticism and collective experimentation.

title: Power Influences Knowledge, but Does Not Make Truth Arbitrary
summary: Power–Knowledge–Truth Test-Cycle: Question → Access → Classification → Evidence → Explanation → Rebuttal → Independent Investigation → Correction → Responsibility Knowledge would not have arisen in a vacuum. Who has the right to ask questions, who has access to libraries/archives, what language is considered “standard,” what data are collected, what expertise gains prestige, what research gets funded, and whose testimony is deemed “credible”—all are influenced by socio-institutional power relations. It would be naïve realism to deny this simple fact. But the second extremism is equally flawed: if power affects knowledge-production, then truth is only a power-made story. In this conclusion, the “social conditions of knowledge” and the “truth-value of claims” are conflated. No government could issue a rain stop order to stop the rains; No university could change historical events by changing vote counts; A company would not be able to eliminate the biological effects of a toxin by renaming the risk. The parallel philosophy separates the entity–knowledge relation into three levels. first, Production-level: question, data, institution, language, wealth, access, methodology. Second, the dissemination-level: publication, forum, (censorship), sequencing, prestige, (pedagogy). Third, truth-testing level: proof, contradiction, (prediction), repeatability-testing, independent confirmation, constraint-evidence. Power can have a huge impact on the first two levels; The third level can also be disrupted, but not completely arbitrary, because claims conflict with world/source/other claims. Wrong (bridge) (design) could collapse, wrong (medical) (dose) damage, (fabricated) date could turn out to be inconsistent with independent archives. “Truth” is not a magical (absolute) (certainty) in this chapter. Truth-claims may be amendable, reliability may be (graded), evidence may be incomplete. (Fallibility) and (arbitrariness) are not the same thing. If I could be wrong, it wouldn't follow that anything would work.
source: Gajendra Thakur’s Parallel Philosophy, Volume II · supplied Maithili Chapter 99 · English translation
purvapaksha: Premise 1: “All knowledge is power-created, so (objective) truth is myth.” Answer: (construction) (production-)Explaining the context, not erasing the truth-condition. (Claim) could be inconsistent with the world/evidence. Premise 2: “The winner would write history, so the story of the defeated is automatically true.” Answer: winner bias real; Defeated sources could provide (counter-)evidence, but not automatically (infallible). Both sources need criticism. Premise 3: “Experts are (elite); people-experience is superior.” Answer: local (experience) opening unseen sides; For complex causal inference, (specialised) methods might be necessary. (Collaborative) (expertise) better. Premise 4: “Data unbiased, fiction biased.” Answer: Influenced by data (collection), (coding), (missingness), (denominator), model selection (value/assumption); Yet the (transparent) measurement would bind more than just the story. Premise 5: “Every truth claim is a power-holding, so (neutral) (adjudication) is impossible.” Answer: Complete (neutrality) Difficult; (comparative) (procedural) (fairness) possible—open proof, (recusal), right of reconsideration, argument-(giving), Independent review.
synthesis: “Power influences knowledge, not arbitrariness of truth” is the balancing formula of this chapter. Power could change whose questions should be heard, whose sources should survive, whose language should be prestigious, whose evidence should be circulated. Here, power-criticism is an essential part of epistemology. But abandoning the concept of truth would not protect the weak; On the contrary, the powerful person could say, “My truth” enough. Justice requires shared factual (adjudication), (documented) evidence, contradiction testing, independent confirmation and correction mechanisms. Parallel philosophy here choosing (neither) (naive) (objectivism) (nor) (total) (relativism). Its ideal is “situated, modifiable, multiproof objectivity”—one that accepts its place/interest/language, but does not abandon the standard for the same reason. Chapter 96 teaching self-criticism, Chapter 97 saying structure is not destiny, Chapter 98 not treating language as a prison at borders, and Chapter 99 preventing truth from becoming arbitrary while acknowledging the real relation of entity-knowledge.

title: Parallel Philosophy: Reconstruction after Deconstruction
summary: Final Test-Cycle: Question → Evidence → Opposition → Language/Structure/Entity-Check → Human Consequences → Self-Review → Revision → Re-examination This chapter is not a summary of previous philosophers. Its goal is to present parallel philosophy as an independent, error-correctable, and publicly testable philosophical method after the lengthy debates of both volumes. Volume–1 yields seven bases; Volume II puts these foundations to a rigorous test with questions of language, structure, fragmentation, power, identity, digitality and artificial intelligence. The last assertion is meaningful only if it can re-examine its previous conclusions. Parallel philosophy does not mean establishing another center. The goal of this project is not to become a permanent “alternative stream” against the term “mainstream” and then become the same type of intellectual monopoly. Its allegiance is not to a permanent camp, but to evidence, truth, dignity, justice, free conscience and self-criticism.
source: Gajendra Thakur’s Parallel Philosophy, Volume II · supplied Maithili Chapter 100 · English translation
synthesis: The seven foundations from Volume–1, the challenge of language/structure/power/fragmentation/artificial intelligence from Volume–2, and self-review, doership, linguistic boundaries and power–truth balance from (Chapters) 96–99—all emerge in Chapter 100 as a system of mutual correction. The philosophical contribution of parallel philosophy is not to provide a new final answer, but to create a public discipline of questioning in which multiple sources, resistance to reality, dignity, power, history, faith, technology and self-criticism test each other's limits. After this final chapter, the book's readers are left with open questions: what claims hold up to the criterion of this method, what modifications are demanded, and what future evidence has the right to change these formulas? Answer to Parallel Philosophy—This right will always be held by future proof and better reasoning.
